articles.author: Elyvora US
articles.description:
If you've ever poked around a website's source code or typed random URLs, you've probably seen robots.txt. That's the file telling search engine bots what they can and can't crawl. But there's another file most people have never heard of: humans.txt.
It's basically robots.txt's friendlier cousin. Instead of talking to bots, it talks to anyone curious enough to look. Maybe you never saw one, but crawlers will surely see it.
It's a text file that lives at yoursite.com/humans.txt. That's it. No fancy format, no technical requirements beyond being plain text. The idea is simple: give credit to the people who built your site and explain what tools you used.
The concept comes from humanstxt.org, a loose standard that started around 2011. It never became an official internet standard like robots.…
articles.title: The humans.txt file: showing there's real people behind your website

articles.author: Spaces Not Tabs
articles.description:
takes a SDF ray marching scene from a fragment shader and does a stylized SVG render, for my pen plotter machine
the goal is to quickly and easily create a nice scene with an SDF in the fragment shader (lol) and then convert into a pen plotter-friendly SVG from it.  Also, add some details that attempt to give depth to volumes and a sense of distance.
this works by first rendering the SDF in a shader in 3 different versions.  First, the scene is rendered using surface normals.  Second, the scene is rendered with distance information.  Third, the scene is rendered based on unique objects.  With these three buffers, I perform marching squares in various ways to highlight the silhouettes and faces of shapes.  Last, I draw random lines around the scene which are meant to give a sense of shape, depth and distance to objects in the scene.
the final export is an svg file for an A4 paper
inspired by the art style of Moebius
articles.title: svg-sdf-art

articles.author: Vipin Yadav
articles.description:
Optimizing Docker Images: From Gigabytes to Megabytes


Docker images bloating to several gigabytes? Your container deployments taking forever? Multi-stage builds are the key to shrinking images, as seen in this transition from 1.2GB to 120MB.
Standard Dockerfile builds include everything: build tools, dev dependencies, source files, and compilation artifacts. Your production container doesn't need any of that.
Before (1.2GB):
FROM node:18
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]


Multi-stage builds allow the use of multiple FROM statements. Each stage can copy artifacts from previous stages while leaving behind everything else.
After (120MB):
# Stage 1: Build
FROM node:18 AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN…
articles.title: How I Reduced My Docker Image Size by 90% Using Multi-Stage Builds
